**Juice Newton** (born **Judith Kay Newton**; February 18, 1952) is an American [pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_music "Pop music") and [country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_music "Country music") singer, songwriter, and musician. Newton has received five [Grammy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award "Grammy Award") nominations in the Pop and Country Best Female Vocalist categories–winning once in 1983–as well as an [ACM Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Country_Music_Awards "Academy of Country Music Awards") for Top New Female Artist and two consecutive _[Billboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard\_(magazine) "Billboard (magazine)")_ Female Album Artist of the Year awards. Newton's other awards include a People's Choice Award for "Best Female Vocalist" and the Australian Music Media's "Number One International Country Artist".

Newton has several Gold and Platinum records to her credit, including _[Juice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juice\_(Juice\_Newton\_album) "Juice (Juice Newton album)")_, _[Quiet Lies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quiet\_Lies "Quiet Lies")_ and her first _Greatest Hits_ album. During the 1980s, she charted 14 top 10 hits across the _Billboard_[Country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot_Country_Songs "Hot Country Songs"), [AC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adult_Contemporary_(chart) "Adult Contemporary (chart)"), and [Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100") charts, with many of the recordings achieving crossover success and six of the songs hitting the No.1 position.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juice_Newton#cite_note-charts-2)

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Juice_Newton&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Newton was born in [Lakehurst, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lakehurst,_New_Jersey "Lakehurst, New Jersey").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juice_Newton#cite_note-3) She is the daughter of a Navy officer.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juice_Newton#cite_note-people-4) Her mother encouraged her interest in music, giving her a guitar for her 13th birthday.

After graduating from [First Colonial High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Colonial_High_School "First Colonial High School") in [Virginia Beach, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia_Beach,_Virginia "Virginia Beach, Virginia"),[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juice_Newton#cite_note-people-4) she attended [Foothill College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foothill_College "Foothill College") in [Los Altos Hills, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Altos_Hills,_California "Los Altos Hills, California"). During this time, she performed [folk music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk_music "Folk music") in some local coffeehouses. She then formed a [folk-rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk-rock "Folk-rock") band with guitarist and songwriter [Otha Young](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otha_Young "Otha Young") and toured bars in Northern California with her band.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juice_Newton#cite_note-AllMusic-5)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Juice_Newton&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

### Early music career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Juice_Newton&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Early music career")]

In the early 1970s, Newton, [Otha Young](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otha_Young "Otha Young") and Tom Kealey formed a band that would eventually be called [Juice Newton & Silver Spur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juice_Newton_&_Silver_Spur "Juice Newton & Silver Spur"), which was signed to [RCA Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Records "RCA Records"). The group released two albums for RCA, in 1975 and 1976, but scored only one charting country single with "Love Is a Word". The band was dropped by RCA, then joined [Capitol Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capitol_Records "Capitol Records") in 1977. The band broke up shortly after releasing just one more album.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juice_Newton#cite_note-AllMusic-5)

In late 1977, Newton went solo, continuing to record for Capitol, and until 1982 Silver Spur remained the name of her backing band. Newton also sang backing vocals for three tracks on [Bob Welch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Welch_(musician) "Bob Welch (musician)")'s platinum solo debut album, including his hit "[Ebony Eyes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ebony_Eyes_(Bob_Welch_song) "Ebony Eyes (Bob Welch song)")".

Near the end of 1977, "[It's a Heartache](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_a_Heartache "It's a Heartache")" became Newton's first solo record and a major hit in Mexico, where it was eventually certified Gold, and in 1978, she released it in the United States. “It’s a Heartache” was the first of Newton's eleven singles to chart on the [_Billboard_ Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100"). Also in 1978, [The Carpenters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Carpenters "The Carpenters")' version of the Newton/Young-penned song "[Sweet, Sweet Smile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweet,_Sweet_Smile "Sweet, Sweet Smile")" reached the Top 10 on both the Country and Adult Contemporary charts, and No. 44 on the _Billboard_ Hot 100.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juice_Newton#cite_note-charts-2) In 1978, Newton legally changed her name from "Judy Kay Newton" to "Juice Newton" ("Juice" having long been her nickname).

Newton's solo debut album, _Well Kept Secret_, was released later in 1978. Neither _Well Kept Secret_ nor its sole single, "Hey Baby", charted, but Capitol Records did renew Newton's contract. In 1979 Capitol's investment in Newton began to pay off as Newton had her first Top-40 Country hit with "Let's Keep It That Way" (another one-off single). Later that year, the album _[Take Heart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Take\_Heart\_(Juice\_Newton\_album) "Take Heart (Juice Newton album)")_ featured five modestly charting singles: "Until Tonight", "[Any Way That You Want Me](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Any_Way_That_You_Want_Me "Any Way That You Want Me")", "You Fill My Life", "[Lay Back in the Arms of Someone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lay_Back_in_the_Arms_of_Someone "Lay Back in the Arms of Someone")", and "[Sunshine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunshine_(Jonathan_Edwards_song) "Sunshine (Jonathan Edwards song)")". In 1980, "Sunshine" became Newton's second top-40 country chart single, "You Fill My Life" reached No. 41, and "Until Tonight" was No. 42.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juice_Newton#cite_note-charts-2) Both of Newton's initial solo efforts performed with modest success but failed to have lasting impacts on the album charts.

### Early 1980s pop music success

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Juice_Newton&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Early 1980s pop music success")]

In 1981, Newton's third solo album, simply titled _Juice_, was released. It spawned three consecutive Top-10 pop hits, namely "[Angel of the Morning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angel_of_the_Morning "Angel of the Morning")" (written by [Chip Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chip_Taylor "Chip Taylor")), "[Queen of Hearts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen_of_Hearts_(Hank_DeVito_song)#Juice_Newton_version "Queen of Hearts (Hank DeVito song)")," and an updated version of "[The Sweetest Thing (I've Ever Known)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sweetest_Thing_(I've_Ever_Known) "The Sweetest Thing (I've Ever Known)")" (the original version had appeared on the Silver Spur debut album), which earned Newton the first of several No. 1 Country chart singles. A fourth single, "[Ride 'Em Cowboy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ride_'Em_Cowboy_(song) "Ride 'Em Cowboy (song)")", from _Juice_ was released in 1984 to support Newton's first _Greatest Hits_ album, reaching the Billboard Country Top 40 chart.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juice_Newton#cite_note-charts-2)

In 1981, Newton's video for "Angel of the Morning" was the first country-music video to air on MTV, the third by a female solo artist (after videos by [Pat Benatar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pat_Benatar "Pat Benatar") and [Carly Simon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carly_Simon "Carly Simon")), and the 40th to air on the channel overall.

_Juice_ sold more than a million copies in the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") and went Triple-Platinum (300,000 copies) in [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada "Canada"). "Angel of the Morning" and "[The Sweetest Thing (I've Ever Known)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sweetest_Thing_(I've_Ever_Known) "The Sweetest Thing (I've Ever Known)")" each reached No. 1 on the Billboard Adult Contemporary chart, where Newton would chart regularly for the next several years. In 1982, Newton received two Grammy nominations for Best Female Vocalist: one for "Angel of the Morning" in the Pop category, and another for "Queen of Hearts" in Country.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juice_Newton#cite_note-bio-6)

These two singles became her biggest sellers in the United States, each earning an [RIAA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recording_Industry_Association_of_America "Recording Industry Association of America") Gold certification. (In 1981 and 1982, when these singles were certified, the RIAA standard for Gold singles was "more than 1 million copies sold"; in 1989, RIAA lowered the standard to 500,000 for Gold single certifications.) The songs were also sizable hits in Canada, Australia, Germany, the Netherlands, and other countries. For example, "Angel of the Morning" peaked at No. 1 in Canada and No. 43 in the [UK Singles Chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UK_Singles_Chart "UK Singles Chart") in 1981.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juice_Newton#cite_note-British_Hit_Singles_&_Albums-7) While "The Sweetest Thing (I've Ever Known)" did not receive a U.S. certification, the song's popularity propelled album sales from Gold to Platinum, and the recording remained in the Top 40 (of the Hot 100) for 18 weeks.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juice_Newton#cite_note-bio-6) "Shot Full Of Love" was released as a single in the UK, but failed to chart.

In the spring of 1982 Newton released her fourth solo album, _[Quiet Lies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quiet\_Lies "Quiet Lies")_, which sold 900,000 copies in the United States. The album went platinum in Canada (100,000 copies). It spawned the Top 10 Pop and Adult Contemporary hit "[Love's Been a Little Bit Hard on Me](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love's_Been_a_Little_Bit_Hard_on_Me "Love's Been a Little Bit Hard on Me")" (which garnered her another Pop Female Vocalist Grammy nomination). "[Break It to Me Gently](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Break_It_to_Me_Gently "Break It to Me Gently")" was the second single and hit No. 1 on the Billboard Adult Contemporary chart, No. 2 on the Billboard Country chart, as well as No. 9 in Cash Box and No. 11 on the [Billboard Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100"). The recording, a contemporary remake of a [Brenda Lee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brenda_Lee "Brenda Lee") hit from the 1960s, won Newton her first [Grammy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award "Grammy Award") for Best Female Country Vocal Performance, beating out contemporaries [Dolly Parton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dolly_Parton "Dolly Parton"), [Rosanne Cash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosanne_Cash "Rosanne Cash"), [Emmylou Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmylou_Harris "Emmylou Harris") and [Sylvia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sylvia_(singer) "Sylvia (singer)"). The album's third and final single, "Heart of the Night," reached No. 4 on the Adult Contemporary chart in early 1983 and climbed to No. 25 on the Hot 100.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juice_Newton#cite_note-charts-2)

The album also garnered Newton an award from Australia as the "Top International Country Artist" for the continent. In 1982, Newton toured with country band [Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alabama_(American_band) "Alabama (American band)") on the "Salem Spirit" double-headliner tour. (Various acts opened for Newton and Alabama.)

The direction for Newton's sixth and final Capitol album, 1983's _Dirty Looks_, was decidedly more rock-oriented and experimental than her usual blending of folk, pop and country styles. The album spawned a moderate-sized hit with "Tell Her No" (Hot 100 No.27/AC No.14) and the title track, a rock-edged number that charted low in the Hot 100. The single "Stranger at My Door" had a brief run on the country chart. The album was a moderate success, selling more than 300,000 copies in the United States and going Gold in Canada (50,000 copies).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juice_Newton#cite_note-8) (The song "Dirty Looks" was written by Dave Robbins and Van Stephenson, who would later become part of the Country group Blackhawk in the 1990s. The pair also wrote Newton's 1984 country single "Restless Heart.")

According to a 1984 front-page article in _Billboard_ magazine, changes at Capitol led Newton to return to RCA. The 1984 album _Can't Wait All Night_ continued with a rock-oriented sound. The launch single, "A Little Love," and the title track became Newton's final charting pop singles to date, reaching No.44 and No.66, respectively, while "Restless Heart" made No.57 on the country chart. "A Little Love" became Newton's seventh and final Top-10 hit on Billboard's Adult Contemporary chart, reaching the No.7 spot.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juice_Newton#cite_note-charts-2) Newton's final double-header "Salem Spirit" tour with Alabama took place during this time, with Bill Medley of [The Righteous Brothers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Righteous_Brothers "The Righteous Brothers") as the opening act.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juice_Newton#cite_note-9)

### From pop to country

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Juice_Newton&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: From pop to country")]

Newton had always been moderately popular in country music; she responded to her waning popularity in the pop market by targeting her next album, 1985's _Old Flame_, solely to country audiences. The strategic move was a success; the album revitalized her career, reached No.12 on the Billboard album chart and featured six Top-10 country hits, including the No.1s "[You Make Me Want to Make You Mine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/You_Make_Me_Want_to_Make_You_Mine "You Make Me Want to Make You Mine")", "[Hurt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurt_(Roy_Hamilton_song) "Hurt (Roy Hamilton song)")", and "[Both to Each Other](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friends_and_Lovers_(Gloria_Loring_and_Carl_Anderson_song) "Friends and Lovers (Gloria Loring and Carl Anderson song)") (Friends and Lovers)" (with [Eddie Rabbitt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddie_Rabbitt "Eddie Rabbitt")), none of which (unlike her previous efforts) appeared at all on the pop charts.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juice_Newton#cite_note-charts-2) The duet was released to the public before the pop version "Friends and Lovers" by [Gloria Loring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gloria_Loring "Gloria Loring") and [Carl Anderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Anderson_(singer) "Carl Anderson (singer)"); the pop version was released to radio and stores two weeks after Newton and Rabbitt's version first appeared, even though it was recorded first. Newton's version was originally available only on a special edition of the _Old Flame_ album and on the Eddie Rabbitt album _Rabbitt Traxx_. The "Old Flame" album produced hit singles for more than sixteen months, with the final release being "What Can I Do with My Heart" (written by Otha Young), which reached the Top 10 in early 1987.

Newton returned to the Top 10 in 1988 with "Tell Me True" from her 1987 album _Emotion_. The album's lead single, the progressive-country tune "First Time Caller", stalled at No.24. Her final album of the decade, _Ain't Gonna Cry_ (1989), was not promoted by the label and did not chart. But it did spawn her final Top-40 country hit to date, "When Love Comes Around the Bend",[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juice_Newton#cite_note-charts-2) which RCA refused to release as a single because Newton's contract had not been renewed.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

After being dropped by RCA Records in 1989 (along with several other country artists, including [Dolly Parton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dolly_Parton "Dolly Parton") and [Kenny Rogers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenny_Rogers "Kenny Rogers"), as country music as a whole was about to undergo momentous change), Newton took time to focus on her family life. Newton took a hiatus from recording albums, touring sporadically until returning to the music scene in late 1990s when she released the albums _[The Trouble with Angels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Trouble\_with\_Angels\_(Juice\_Newton\_album) "The Trouble with Angels (Juice Newton album)")_ (1998) and _[American Girl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American\_Girl\_(album) "American Girl (album)")_ (1999).[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juice_Newton#cite_note-disc-10)

### 1990s to present

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Juice_Newton&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: 1990s to present")]

In 1994, Newton contributed the track "Lovers of One Day" to an [Édith Piaf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89dith_Piaf "Édith Piaf") tribute album which also included songs by [Pat Benatar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pat_Benatar "Pat Benatar") and [Donna Summer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donna_Summer "Donna Summer").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juice_Newton#cite_note-11)

In 1995, Newton recorded a double album of pop duets (which was slated to be sold via [infomercial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infomercial "Infomercial")), but the project was riddled with legal issues, resulting in a low-impact, "accidental" release of the "Platinum & Gold" series of duets in the early 2000s (the CD set was released without Newton's permission). Subsequently, bootleg CDs including most of the duets turned up on U.S. store shelves as _Gold & Platinum, Volumes 7 and 8_. Those CDs also contain 1995 solo versions of three of Newton's pop hits: "Angel of the Morning", "Love's Been a Little Bit Hard on Me" and "Queen of Hearts". Newton's duet partners included [Willie Nelson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Nelson "Willie Nelson"), [Melissa Manchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melissa_Manchester "Melissa Manchester"), [The Pointer Sisters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pointer_Sisters "The Pointer Sisters") and [Frankie Valli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frankie_Valli "Frankie Valli"). In 1998, Newton released _The Trouble with Angels_, a collection of seven re-recorded hits and three new songs, including the single "When I Get Over You". The 1998 effort was quickly followed by _American Girl_ in 1999, which was Newton's first album of all-new material since 1989 and featured the single "They Never Made It to Memphis". The collection featured tracks written by Otha Young, [Freddie Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freddie_Mercury "Freddie Mercury"), [Nanci Griffith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanci_Griffith "Nanci Griffith"), [Tom Petty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Petty "Tom Petty") and Newton herself.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juice_Newton#cite_note-12)

_[Every Road Leads Back to You](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Every\_Road\_Leads\_Back\_to\_You "Every Road Leads Back to You")_ (which consists of live material and a bonus EP of four studio recordings of original songs) was released in 2002 with an accompanying DVD. _American Girl Vol. II_, which was originally sold exclusively at cdbaby.com and at Newton's live shows, was released in 2003 and reissued in 2006 and again in 2011 by Brookside Records.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juice_Newton#cite_note-disc-10)

In 2005, Newton appeared on the TV show _[Hit Me, Baby, One More Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hit\_Me,\_Baby,\_One\_More\_Time\_(TV\_series) "Hit Me, Baby, One More Time (TV series)")_, on which she performed a folk-rock rendition of "[Pieces Of Me](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pieces_of_Me_(Ashlee_Simpson_song) "Pieces of Me (Ashlee Simpson song)")" and a truncated version of "Queen of Hearts"; online voters selected Newton's performance as their favorite of the five acts that appeared on the episode.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juice_Newton#cite_note-13) In the mid-2000s, Newton also contributed tracks to the albums _An All-Star Tribute To [Cher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cher "Cher")_ ("Reason to Believe") and _An All-Star Tribute to [Shania Twain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shania\_Twain "Shania Twain")_ ("Come On Over").

On November 15, 2007, Newton released _The Gift of Christmas_, her first Christmas album.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juice_Newton#cite_note-14) The 12-song album includes a new version of Newton's "Christmas Needs Love to Be Christmas" and "[Mary's Boy Child](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary's_Boy_Child "Mary's Boy Child")", as well as a special Christmas version of "For Believers", an Otha Young-penned song first recorded in 1983 for the _Dirty Looks_ album.

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3d/JuiceNewtonByPhilKonstantin.jpg/250px-JuiceNewtonByPhilKonstantin.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:JuiceNewtonByPhilKonstantin.jpg)

Juice Newton, San Diego, 2009

On August 6, 2009, Newton's longtime musical partner Otha Young died of cancer. The pair worked together for 37 years.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juice_Newton#cite_note-15)

In 2010, Newton's _Duets: Friends & Memories_ album was released by Fuel 2000.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juice_Newton#cite_note-16) The album contained duets performed with [Willie Nelson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Nelson "Willie Nelson"), [Melissa Manchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melissa_Manchester "Melissa Manchester"), [Frankie Valli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frankie_Valli "Frankie Valli") and others. One single ("Funny How Time Slips Away") was released.

In 2011, Fuel 2000 released _Juice Newton: The Ultimate Hits Collection_, which included her own version of the Carpenters' 1978 hit "Sweet Sweet Smile", which Newton and Otha Young wrote in the '70s.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juice_Newton#cite_note-17)

In 2012, BGO Records issued a two-CD set containing Newton's three 1970s Capitol albums: _Come To Me_, _Well Kept Secret_ and _Take Heart_.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juice_Newton#cite_note-18) This marked the first time these albums have been available in the CD format. With the release of this set, all Newton's 17 studio albums have been issued on CD.

In the 2016 film _[Deadpool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deadpool\_(film) "Deadpool (film)")_, Newton's version of "Angel of the Morning" was used for the opening credits montage.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juice_Newton#cite_note-19) As a result, the track re-charted on the Billboard Country chart, reaching No. 43, and also hit No. 3 on Spotify's World Music chart. In 2020, Newton's version of "Angel of the Morning" was featured in the film _[Promising Young Woman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Promising\_Young\_Woman "Promising Young Woman")_.

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Juice_Newton&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Newton bought a thoroughbred [gelding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gelding "Gelding") named Puppy in 1983[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juice_Newton#cite_note-people-4) and stabled him at the [Los Angeles Equestrian Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Equestrian_Center "Los Angeles Equestrian Center"). The center's manager was [polo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polo "Polo") star and coach Tom Goodspeed. Newton married Goodspeed in 1985. They have two children: Jessica and Tyler.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juice_Newton#cite_note-people-4)

Besides continuing in the music business, Newton works as a horse trader, dealing mostly in European breeds.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juice_Newton#cite_note-20) She also played polo herself.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juice_Newton#cite_note-people-4)

_**The Unforgettable Fire**_ is the fourth studio album by Irish [rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music") band [U2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U2 "U2"). It was produced by [Brian Eno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Eno "Brian Eno") and [Daniel Lanois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Lanois "Daniel Lanois"), and released on 1 October 1984 by [Island Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Island_Records "Island Records"). The band wanted to pursue a new musical direction following the harder-hitting rock of their previous album, _[War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War\_(U2\_album) "War (U2 album)")_ (1983). As a result, they employed Eno and Lanois to produce and assist in their experimentation with a more [ambient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambient_music "Ambient music") sound. The resulting change in direction was at the time the band's most dramatic. The album's title is a reference to "The Unforgettable Fire", an art exhibit about the [atomic bombing of Hiroshima](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_bombing_of_Hiroshima "Atomic bombing of Hiroshima").

Recording began in May 1984 at [Slane Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slane_Castle "Slane Castle"), where the band lived, wrote, and recorded to find new inspiration. The album was completed in August 1984 at [Windmill Lane Studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Windmill_Lane_Studios "Windmill Lane Studios"). It features atmospheric sounds and lyrics that lead vocalist [Bono](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bono "Bono") describes as "sketches". "[Pride (In the Name of Love)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pride_(In_the_Name_of_Love) "Pride (In the Name of Love)")" and "[MLK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MLK_(song) "MLK (song)")" are lyrical tributes to [Martin Luther King Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Luther_King_Jr. "Martin Luther King Jr.")[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-2)

_The Unforgettable Fire_ received generally favourable reviews from critics and produced the band's biggest hit at the time, "Pride (In the Name of Love)", as well as the live favourite "[Bad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bad_(U2_song) "Bad (U2 song)")". A 25th anniversary edition of the album was released in October 2009.

## Background

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Unforgettable_Fire&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")]

> "We knew the world was ready to receive the heirs to [the Who](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Who "The Who"). All we had to do was to keep doing what we were doing and we would become the biggest band since [Led Zeppelin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Led_Zeppelin "Led Zeppelin"), without a doubt. But something just didn't feel right. We felt we had more dimension than just the next big anything, we had something unique to offer. The innovation was what would suffer if we went down the standard rock route. We were looking for another feeling."

—Bono, on _The Unforgettable Fire'_ s new direction.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-McCormick_2006,_p._147-3)

U2 feared that following the overt rock of their 1983 album _[War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War\_(U2\_album) "War (U2 album)")_ and the [War Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_Tour "War Tour"), they were in danger of becoming another "shrill", "sloganeering [arena-rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arena-rock "Arena-rock") band".[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-RS_JT-4) Following their concert at Dublin's [Phoenix Park Racecourse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenix_Park_Racecourse "Phoenix Park Racecourse") in August 1983, one of the final dates of the War Tour, lead vocalist [Bono](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bono "Bono") spoke in metaphors about the group breaking up and reforming with a different direction. In the 10th issue of _U2 Magazine_, released in February 1984, Bono hinted at radical changes on the next album saying that he could not "sleep at night with the thought of it all" and that they were "undertaking a real departure".[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-McGee74-5) As bassist [Adam Clayton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adam_Clayton "Adam Clayton") recalls, "We were looking for something that was a bit more serious, more arty."[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-McCormick_2006,_p._147-3)

After completing the War Tour in Japan late that year,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-6) U2 rehearsed at Bono's seaside home in a [Martello tower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martello_tower "Martello tower") in [Bray, County Wicklow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bray,_County_Wicklow "Bray, County Wicklow"). During this time, early versions of the songs "[Pride (In the Name of Love)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pride_(In_the_Name_of_Love) "Pride (In the Name of Love)")", "[The Unforgettable Fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire_(song) "The Unforgettable Fire (song)")", and "[A Sort of Homecoming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Sort_of_Homecoming_(song) "A Sort of Homecoming (song)")" were composed.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-McCormick_2006,_p._147-3)

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8f/Martello_Tower_in_Bray.jpg/250px-Martello_Tower_in_Bray.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Martello_Tower_in_Bray.jpg)

The group wrote initial material for the album at Bono's home in a [Martello tower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martello_tower "Martello tower") in late 1983.

U2 had recorded their first three albums at [Windmill Lane Studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Windmill_Lane_Studios "Windmill Lane Studios") but decided to find a new location for their next studio album.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-mcc148-7) Clayton lamented the lack of a live room in which the band could play together at Windmill Lane,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-McGee75-8) while the band's manager [Paul McGuinness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_McGuinness "Paul McGuinness") said the studio had barely enough space for people to work.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-mcc148-7) He set to finding a new location and came up with Church Hall in [Ranelagh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ranelagh "Ranelagh"), but he found it overpriced.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-mcc148-7) The band's tour manager Dennis Sheehan also searched for suitable locations and found [Slane Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slane_Castle "Slane Castle") in [County Meath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_Meath "County Meath").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-questforfire-9) The building's owner, Lord [Henry Mountcharles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Mountcharles "Henry Mountcharles"), offered to lease it to the group for less than half the cost of Church Hall, and also offered lodging and dining for the band and crew on-premises.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-mcc148-7) The castle's [Gothic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gothic_architecture "Gothic architecture") ballroom, which was originally built for music and had a 30-foot high domed ceiling, also attracted the band, as they were looking to capture the natural acoustics of a room in their recordings.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-mcc148-7)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-Jamming-10)

After working with [producer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Record_producer "Record producer")[Steve Lillywhite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Lillywhite "Steve Lillywhite") on their first three albums, the band sought experimentation rather than to create the "son of _War_".[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-Graham_1996,_p._21-11) Both Lillywhite and the group agreed that it was time for a change of producers and that they should not "repeat the same formula".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-McCormick_2006,_p._147-3) For their next studio album, the band considered hiring [Conny Plank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conny_Plank "Conny Plank"), whose previous production credits included [Can](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Can_(band) "Can (band)"), [Kraftwerk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kraftwerk "Kraftwerk"), and [Ultravox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ultravox "Ultravox").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-12) U2 also met with [Roxy Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roxy_Music "Roxy Music") producer [Rhett Davies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhett_Davies "Rhett Davies"), but Clayton said that it "didn't really go anywhere".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-McCormick_2006,_p._147-3) They also considered [Jimmy Iovine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Iovine "Jimmy Iovine"), who had produced their live album _[Under a Blood Red Sky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Under\_a\_Blood\_Red\_Sky "Under a Blood Red Sky")_ in 1983,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-job115-13) but they found their early musical ideas for the new album to be too "European" for an American producer.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-McGee75-8) Iovine thought that he was in line for the job and went so far as to hold a meeting about recording logistics at Slane Castle with his [engineer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audio_engineering "Audio engineering")[Shelly Yakus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shelly_Yakus "Shelly Yakus") and with another engineer Randy Ezratty, whose mobile recording studio U2 would be using once again. However, at the last minute, McGuinness informed Ezratty that they would be proceeding with different producers.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-job115-13)

[![Image 6: Headshots of Brian Eno and Daniel Lanois.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/68/Brian_Eno_and_Daniel_Lanois.jpg/250px-Brian_Eno_and_Daniel_Lanois.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Brian_Eno_and_Daniel_Lanois.jpg)

Seeking a new musical direction after their first three albums, U2 hired [Brian Eno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Eno "Brian Eno") and [Daniel Lanois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Lanois "Daniel Lanois") to produce _The Unforgettable Fire_.

U2 instead had turned their attention to hiring musician/producer [Brian Eno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Eno "Brian Eno"). Guitarist [the Edge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Edge "The Edge") had long admired Eno's music,[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-14) particularly his [ambient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambient_music "Ambient music") and "weird works".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-McCormick_2006,_p._147-3) The group were also fond of his collaborations with [Talking Heads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talking_Heads "Talking Heads").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-Graham_1996,_p._21-11) Eno was hesitant to work with a rock band and when contacted by U2, he told them he was considering retiring from music production to become a video artist.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-job115-13)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-mcc148-7) Reluctantly, Eno agreed to meet with the band in Dublin and brought along his engineer [Daniel Lanois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Lanois "Daniel Lanois") with the intention of recommending he work with them instead;[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-mcc148-7) Lanois had his own ambitions of producing a rock band.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-pitchfork-eno-lanois-15) When the band played _Under a Blood Red Sky_ to Eno, his eyes "glazed over".[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-mcc148-7) The Edge said of him: "I think he was intimidated by the lack of irony in what we were doing. He'd come from Talking Heads, the [Rhode Island School of Design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhode_Island_School_of_Design "Rhode Island School of Design"), living in New York, and here was this Irish band hitting everything full on, completely earnest, hearts on sleeves, no irony at all."[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-16) Eno also thought that the group were "frightened of being overpowered by some softness". His doubts were resolved by Bono's persuasiveness and his increasing perception of what he called "U2's lyrical soul in abundance".[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-Graham_1996,_p._21-11) Eno was impressed by how they spoke, which was not in terms of music or playing, but in terms of their contributions to the "identity of the band as a whole".[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-McGee74-5) The band's discussion about pursuing different recording techniques and capturing the ambience of a recording space also piqued his interest.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-mcc148-7) Ultimately, Eno and Lanois agreed to produce the record with the understanding that if Eno's working relationship with U2 was not fruitful, they would still have a solid producer in Lanois on which they could fall back.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-pitchfork-eno-lanois-15)

[Island Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Island_Records "Island Records") founder [Chris Blackwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Blackwell "Chris Blackwell") initially tried to talk U2 out of hiring Eno, believing that just when they were about to achieve the highest levels of success, Eno would "bury them under a layer of avant-garde nonsense".[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-U2byU2_151-17) Nick Stewart, also of Island Records, thought the band were "mad".[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-McGee74-5) Blackwell instructed him to dissuade U2 from working with Eno; Stewart recalled Blackwell telling him, "You better sort your band out because they're going in a very odd direction." Stewart was unable to change their minds, prompting Blackwell to fly to Dublin to meet with the group.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-job115-13) Ultimately, Blackwell too was convinced by Bono's persuasiveness and the band's enthusiasm for the collaboration.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-mcc148-7)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-job115-13) Stewart said that in hindsight, the group's decision to stretch themselves and find an extra dimension became the "turning point in their career".[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-McGee74-5)

## Recording and production

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Unforgettable_Fire&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Recording and production")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f2/2013_at_Slane_Castle_%288647010098%29.jpg/250px-2013_at_Slane_Castle_%288647010098%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:2013_at_Slane_Castle_(8647010098).jpg)

The first phase of recording took place in [Slane Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slane_Castle "Slane Castle").

The band arrived at Slane Castle on 7 May 1984 for a month-long recording session.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-McGee75-8) A makeshift control room was set up in the castle's drawing room.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-job115-13) Ezratty's company Effanel Music, which recorded U2's concerts in Boston and at [Red Rocks Amphitheatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Rocks_Amphitheatre "Red Rocks Amphitheatre") the previous year, was hired to provide their then-unique portable 24-track recording system.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-McGee75-8) The equipment, which came in wheeling [flight cases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_case "Road case") with removable lids, was described by Lanois as a "heavily modified Sound Workshop [mixing console](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixing_console "Mixing console") with a Stevens[_[sic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sic "Sic")_] tape recorder". He said it was not the "ultimate technical system" but that the priority was to capture the feeling of the band's music.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-sos-sep87-18) Ezratty's equipment was set up in the castle's library, dubbed the Chinese Room, with cables running into the adjacent ballroom where the band played.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-McGee75-8)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-pluckofirish-19) The band and crew lived at the castle during the sessions, helping to foster a camaraderie among them.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-reuters-20) The site provided a relaxed and experimental atmosphere.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-STOKES_50-51-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-Graham_1996,_p._23-22)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-Jamming-10)

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e3/Bono_and_the_Edge_on_Unforgettable_Fire_Tour_in_Sydney_9-9-84.jpg/250px-Bono_and_the_Edge_on_Unforgettable_Fire_Tour_in_Sydney_9-9-84.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bono_and_the_Edge_on_Unforgettable_Fire_Tour_in_Sydney_9-9-84.jpg)

The Edge and Bono were receptive to producer Brian Eno's experimental approach.

U2 worked long days at the castle, sometimes starting at 10 a.m. and finishing at 1 a.m. Eno, who worked on a more "executive schedule" than other members of the creative team,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-job115-13) was focused on creative ideas and conceptual aspects, while Lanois handled the production duties.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-pitchfork-eno-lanois-15) In Bill Graham's words, Eno's task was to "help [U2] mature a new, more experimental and European musical vocabulary".[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-23) Eno was glad that the group began the sessions with only rough sketches of songs, as he was more interested in encouraging experimentation and improvisation than refining their ideas. To that end, he often created atmospheric compositions on a synthesiser that were intended to inspire U2 and Lanois to play along with.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-job115-13) Bono and the Edge, who the singer described as the "more cerebral" members of the band, were particularly drawn to Eno's ideas.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-U2byU2_151-17) The band's experiments produced 15 additional pieces of music.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-job115-13) The Edge said that they "didn't object to [Eno] taking liberties with what [they] had achieved up to that point", adding: "We were eager to learn and not precious at all about our sound or the way we worked. We threw ourselves wholeheartedly into this different approach." According to the Edge, Eno's points of reference were philosophy and [contemporary art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contemporary_art "Contemporary art"), and he was not beholden to the standard schools of thought in rock music.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-U2byU2_151-17) The producer encouraged U2 to work on their more unconventional material,[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-U2byU2_151-17) "champion[ing] the songs that didn't seem very U2-ish or things that had strong beginnings but no clear destination".[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-kingsofcastle-24) As a result, he did not take much interest in songs like "Pride (In the Name of Love)" or "The Unforgettable Fire". Lanois would "cover for him" such that the two balanced each other out.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-U2byU2_151-17)

Since U2 had primarily been interested in working with Eno, Lanois was initially viewed as an "interloper", which caused tension at the start of the sessions, according to Ezratty. Once the band realised his musical talents, they embraced him as a fellow collaborator. As a songwriter and multi-instrumentalist, Lanois understood [musical notation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_notation "Musical notation") and was able to simplify the songwriting process for them. Drummer [Larry Mullen Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Mullen_Jr. "Larry Mullen Jr.") in particular enjoyed working with Lanois, as the producer took an interest in the band's rhythm section, which Mullen felt had been neglected on their past recordings.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-job115-13) Mullen called himself "not technically proficient" and appreciated Lanois spending time to develop his skills and encourage different approaches to playing drums.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-U2byU2_151-17) The producer convinced Mullen to utilise [timbales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timbales "Timbales") and two types of [snare drums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snare_drum "Snare drum") (one being a piccolo snare) in his drum kit, and he explained how to use [brushes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drum_brush "Drum brush") and [tom-toms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom-tom_drum "Tom-tom drum") on various drum parts.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-job115-13)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-pluckofirish-19) The crew also experimented with distant [miking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microphone_practice "Microphone practice") of his drum kit, placing microphones up to 60 feet away. Mullen eschewed wearing headphones while playing and instead used [monitor speakers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stage_monitor_system "Stage monitor system"), which caused [audio spill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audio_spill "Audio spill") issues with other microphones in the recording space.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-pluckofirish-19)

> "With Steve [Lillywhite], we were a lot more strict about a song and what it should be; if it did veer off to the left or the right, we would pull it back as opposed to chasing it. Brian [Eno] and Danny [Lanois] were definitely interested in watching where a song went and then chasing it."

—[Adam Clayton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adam_Clayton "Adam Clayton"), on how _The Unforgettable Fire_'s producers approached the album[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-25)

The Edge said that the band's plan for recording at Slane was rather than working in the "dead, acoustic atmosphere" of a studio and "trying to revitalise the recorded work using effects and reverberation and all the standard music trappings, we would go into a very live room and try to do the opposite—try and tame what would be a wild sound".[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-Jamming-10) To capture the feeling of the music as much as possible, they recorded the basic tracks as live [takes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Take "Take") with the whole band playing together; this differed from their previous albums, for which they [overdubbed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overdub "Overdub") the instruments as separate tracks on top of a drum track, with as much separation as possible. The Edge felt that the "vibrancy" from playing their older songs live had "outshone what [they] had done on record", thus inspiring them to seek out a more live feel for _The Unforgettable Fire_.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-26)

Lanois originally intended for the band to record entirely in the ballroom, which he described as a "beautiful very tall room with big mirrors, chandeliers and windows overlooking the river".[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-sos-sep87-18) Shortly after their arrival, the team realised that the ballroom had too much natural reverberation, necessitating the addition of sound [absorption](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Absorption_(acoustics) "Absorption (acoustics)") materials such as drapes to the walls.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-job115-13) Lanois said the room was only suitable for songs with "openness but not good for tracks that were quick and required punch",[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-sos-sep87-18) while crew member Stephen Rainford said, "Okay for [chamber music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chamber_music "Chamber music"), but no good for rock and roll".[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-job115-13) Consequently, most of the recording took place in the library, which was smaller, rectangular, filled with books, and provided improved sound quality. Lanois said the room helped them "achieve a denser more powerful sound" on their recordings.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-reuters-20)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-sos-sep87-18) Adding to the recording challenges was the [water wheel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water_wheel "Water wheel") generator on [River Boyne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Boyne "River Boyne") that powered the building. During low tide or periods of no rain, there was not sufficient power to keep their recording equipment operational.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-sos-sep87-18)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-job115-13)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-kingsofcastle-24) Ezratty said, "When that stupid river started to run low, the voltage would go down and it would beat the crap out of my equipment." As a backup, the team were forced to make use of an old [diesel generator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diesel_generator "Diesel generator"), which at times broke down or caught fire.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-job115-13)

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/96/Edge_Drammenshallen.jpg/250px-Edge_Drammenshallen.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Edge_Drammenshallen.jpg)

The Edge _(pictured in 1985)_ experimented with his guitar playing style, equipment setup, and tunings during the recording sessions at Eno's encouragement.

The Edge was encouraged by Eno to think of the [studio as an instrument](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recording_studio_as_an_instrument "Recording studio as an instrument") and to expand the range of his guitar tones, resulting in experiments with his equipment and guitar playing techniques.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-job115-13) The producer processed the Edge's guitar through an [AMS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AMS_(Advanced_Music_Systems) "AMS (Advanced Music Systems)")[harmonizer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmonizer "Harmonizer") effects unit, a [Lexicon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lexicon_(company) "Lexicon (company)") Prime Time [delay unit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delay_(audio_effect) "Delay (audio effect)"), and a [reverb chamber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reverberation_room "Reverberation room"); Lanois at times confused the guitar sounds for keyboards.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-pluckofirish-19) The Edge also used an [EBow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EBow "EBow"), a [slide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slide_guitar "Slide guitar") with echo, [alternative guitar tunings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guitar_tunings#Alternative "Guitar tunings"), and a "zero [sustain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sustain "Sustain")" technique that [muted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mute_(music) "Mute (music)") his strings with tape across the [bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bridge_(instrument) "Bridge (instrument)").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-job115-13) He experimented with the placement and miking of his [guitar amplifier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guitar_amplifier "Guitar amplifier"). At times, it was situated outside on the balcony encircling the castle, with close miking and, when it rained, a plastic cover to shield it.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-sos-sep87-18)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-27) This placement was originally done for sound isolation purposes, but ended up producing a good sound.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-sos-sep87-18) Other times, his amplifier was placed at the bottom of a staircase, with one microphone there and another placed at the top of the staircase.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-job115-13)

A [Fairlight CMI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairlight_CMI "Fairlight CMI") synthesiser was used during the demoing phase out of convenience to help fill in placeholder textures and string ideas, marking the first time the instrument had been used on a U2 album. These textures were later replaced with actual string arrangements, although the Fairlight CMI was kept on one song. Clayton said the synthesiser "was only really used as a means to an end, to see if an idea worked".[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-clayton-storey-u2mag-28) Eno contributed synthesiser parts on a Yamaha DX7, while he and the Edge also played a Yamaha CP-70 [electric grand piano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_grand_piano "Electric grand piano").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-pluckofirish-19)

Bono recorded his vocals on [Neumann U47](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neumann_U47 "Neumann U47") and U67 and [AKG](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AKG_(company) "AKG (company)") C-12 microphones. Lanois said that they captured a warm sound and a "bottom end and depth" to Bono's vocals. For "Promenade", one of the first songs for which vocals were recorded, Lanois encouraged Bono to sing quieter by increasing the volume of his vocals in his headphones. By doing so, the producer was able to force Bono to "draw on the fine points of the voice".[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-pluckofirish-19)

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2e/Windmill_Lane_Studio.jpg/250px-Windmill_Lane_Studio.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Windmill_Lane_Studio.jpg)

The second phase of recording took place at [Windmill Lane Studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Windmill_Lane_Studios "Windmill Lane Studios").

The band finished recording at Slane Castle on 5 June and began a second phase of the recording sessions at Windmill Lane Studios the following day.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-McGee75-8) Their original intent was to record the [backing tracks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Backing_track "Backing track") at Slane before overdubbing and [mixing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audio_mixing_(recorded_music) "Audio mixing (recorded music)") at Windmill Lane.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-questforfire-9) Clayton said this was because the mobile recording equipment did not offer them as many options or treatment possibilities as a traditional studio mixing console would.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-clayton-storey-u2mag-28) However, the group ended up crafting their songs at Windmill Lane more than they originally anticipated, including re-recording "Pride (In the Name of Love)".[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-sos-sep87-18) The Edge reflected that when recording at a new location such as Slane, it took them a few weeks to "get in to the momentum of the new creative surrounding".[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-job115-13) Lanois said that in hindsight the recording sessions were "split in a slightly off-balanced fashion", with too much time being dedicated to experimenting and not enough to fundamental recording.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-sos-sep87-18) Within the band, there were concerns that their material recorded at Slane was too skeletal to consider completing yet, prompting them to re-evaluate and in some cases re-record it. Eno, on the other hand, was more interested in recording as few takes as possible and preserving the rough, spontaneous nature of the music.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-job115-13) Clayton said that Eno would get easily bored if he had nothing to do, while Mullen said he was impatient with U2's creative process. Tension grew between them and the production team, largely because the band "weren't at a point where [they] could finish anything".[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-U2byU2_152-29)

Throughout the recording sessions, Bono had been ad-libbing his vocals, without completing lyrics. Mullen explained that the group's reliance on Bono to help complete the musical composition of their songs took time away from him to work on the lyrics independently: "While recording, we seemed to do our best work when we were in the room together. We depended on Bono to be there, every step of the way. He had to be singing something, anything, to get the song finished. When Bono came in and strapped on a guitar or started to sing, the band responded... A song recorded in the room with Bono and a song recorded without him could be very different animals altogether."[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-mcc155-30) Whereas Bono wanted to finalise the lyrics, Eno, Lanois, and the Edge advocated preserving the improvised nature of his vocals, telling the singer, "Why write lyrics?... I'm getting the feeling from this." In retrospect, Bono lamented leaving the lyrics to songs like "Bad" and "Pride (In the Name of Love)" as incomplete "sketches".[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-U2byU2_151-17)

Twelve days before the deadline to complete the record, Bono told his bandmates he did not think he would be able to finish the lyrics in time, creating a panic internally. McGuinness reminded the group of their commitment to tour Australia and New Zealand in less than a month, and that the producers and studio would not be available afterwards.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-job115-13) To complete the album, the band worked 20-hour days for the final two weeks;[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-31) Eno worked the first half of days, while Lanois worked the second half.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-job115-13) Eno departed before the album was completed, leaving Lanois to oversee the final mixes.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-mcc155-30) On their final day in the studio, the band worked overnight to complete the album by 7–8 a.m. on 5 August.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-job115-13)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-McGee75-8)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-musician-sept93-32) As Lanois was preparing to depart for London with the album tapes for [mastering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mastering_(audio) "Mastering (audio)"), Bono expressed interest in recording another take of his vocals for "A Sort of Homecoming". With his taxi to the airport waiting outside, Lanois cued up the tapes for Bono to record one final vocal take. Lanois told the band he would mix it in London and then departed,[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-musician-sept93-32) delivering the tapes for mastering in the basement of Blackwell's offices.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-job115-13)

Portions of the recording sessions were filmed by [Barry Devlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barry_Devlin "Barry Devlin") and his crew for an [RTÉ-TV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RT%C3%89_Television "RTÉ Television") documentary. The 30-minute programme, _The Making of The Unforgettable Fire_, was released in 1985 on VHS as part of _The Unforgettable Fire Collection_.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-McGee75-8) Devlin said that he did not think the band and crew had thought through the logistics and access required for a film crew to document the making of the album. He often encountered "No Entry" signs on doors and windows when attempting to film the group, forcing him to take a more artful, impressionistic approach to the documentary.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-kingsofcastle-24)

## Composition

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Unforgettable_Fire&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Composition")]

A far more atmospheric album than the previous _War_, _The Unforgettable Fire_ was at the time the band's most dramatic change in direction.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-33)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-PARRA_52-56-34) It has a rich and orchestrated sound and was the first U2 album with a cohesive sound.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-PARRA_52-56-34) Under Lanois's direction, Mullen's drumming became looser, funkier and more subtle, and Clayton's bass became more subliminal, such that the rhythm section no longer intruded, but flowed in support of the songs.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-STOKES_50-51-21) Eno's atmospheric production, along with more experimental song structures, lent the album an "art-rock sensibility" and "atmospheric rock" style that departed from U2's "hard-hitting post-punk roots", according to _[Paste](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paste\_(magazine) "Paste (magazine)")_ magazine's Luke Larson.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-35) Both _[Stereogum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stereogum "Stereogum")_[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-36) and _[Entertainment Weekly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entertainment\_Weekly "Entertainment Weekly")_[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-37) also observed art rock on the album, while _[The Austin Chronicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Austin\_Chronicle "The Austin Chronicle")_'s Christopher Gray said "the rich textures, impressionistic tableaux, and cinematic landscapes" may not be "art rock _per se_", but still "served to distance U2 even further from their post-punk peers".[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-38)

The opening track, "[A Sort of Homecoming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Sort_of_Homecoming_(U2_song) "A Sort of Homecoming (U2 song)")", immediately shows the change in U2's sound. Like much of the album, the hard-hitting martial drum sound of _War_ was replaced with a subtler [polyrhythmic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polyrhythm "Polyrhythm")[shuffle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swung_note "Swung note"), and the guitar was no longer as prominent in the mix.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-Graham_1996,_p._23-22) Typical of the album, the track "[The Unforgettable Fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire_(song) "The Unforgettable Fire (song)")", with a string arrangement by [Noel Kelehan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noel_Kelehan "Noel Kelehan"), has a rich, symphonic sound built from ambient guitar and driving rhythm, along with a lyrical "sketch" that is an "emotional travelogue" with a "heartfelt sense of yearning".[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-STOKES_55-39) The band cited a travelling Japanese art exhibit of the same name as inspiration for both the song and album title. The exhibition, which the band attended in Chicago, commemorated the victims of the [bombing of Hiroshima](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_bombings_of_Hiroshima_and_Nagasaki "Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-Stokes_1996,_p._54-40)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-41) However, the open-ended lyric, which Bono says "doesn't tell you anything", does not directly reference nuclear warfare.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-42) Rather, the lyrics are about travelling to Tokyo.

The album's lyrics are open to many interpretations, which alongside its atmospheric sounds, provides what the band often called a "very visual feel".[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-PARRA_52-56-34) Bono had recently been immersing himself in fiction, philosophy and poetry, and came to realise that his song writing mission—which up to that point had been a reluctant one on his behalf—was a poetic one. Bono felt songs like "Bad" and "Pride (In the Name of Love)" were best left as incomplete "sketches",[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-U2byU2_151-17) and he said that "_The Unforgettable Fire_ was a beautifully out-of-focus record, blurred like an [impressionist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impressionism "Impressionism") painting, very unlike a billboard or an advertising slogan."[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-43)

The melody and the chords to "[Pride (In the Name of Love)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pride_(In_the_Name_of_Love) "Pride (In the Name of Love)")" originally came out of a 1983 War Tour sound check in [Hawaii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii "Hawaii"). The song was originally intended to be about [Ronald Reagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Reagan "Ronald Reagan")'s pride in America's military power, but Bono was influenced by [Stephen B. Oates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_B._Oates "Stephen B. Oates")'s book about [Martin Luther King Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Luther_King_Jr. "Martin Luther King Jr.") titled _Let The Trumpet Sound: A Life of Martin Luther King, Jr._ and a biography of [Malcolm X](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malcolm_X "Malcolm X") to ponder the different sides of the civil rights campaigns, the violent and the non-violent.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-44) Bono would revise the lyrics to pay tribute to King. "Pride" went through many changes and re-recordings, as captured in a documentary included on _[The Unforgettable Fire Collection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Unforgettable\_Fire#The\_Unforgettable\_Fire\_Collection)_ video. "Pride" is the most conventional song on the album—Tony Fletcher of _Jamming!_ magazine said at the time it was the most commercial song U2 had written—and it was chosen as the album's first single.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-Jamming-10)

On "Wire" Bono tried to convey his ambivalence to drugs. It is a fast-paced song built on a light funk drum groove.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-Stokes53-45) The song shows the influence of [Talking Heads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talking_Heads "Talking Heads"), with whom Eno had worked.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-46) Much of the song was improvised by Bono at the microphone.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-Stokes53-45)

The ambient instrumental "[4th of July](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4th_of_July_(U2_song) "4th of July (U2 song)")" came about almost entirely through a moment of inspiration from Eno. At the end of a studio session, Eno overheard Clayton improvising a simple bass figure and recorded it "ad hoc" as it was being played. The Edge happened to join in, improvising a few guitar ideas over the top of Clayton's bass; neither knew they were being recorded. Eno added some treatments and then transferred the piece straight to two-track master tape—and that was the song finished, with no possibility of further overdubs.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-47)

Bono tried to describe the rush and then come down of heroin use in the song "[Bad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bad_(U2_song) "Bad (U2 song)")".[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-U2byU2_152-29)

The sparse, dreamlike "[MLK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MLK_(song) "MLK (song)")" was written as an [elegy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elegy "Elegy") to King.

## Release and promotion

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Unforgettable_Fire&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Release and promotion")]

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4a/Moydrum_Castle.jpg/250px-Moydrum_Castle.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Moydrum_Castle.jpg)

[Moydrum Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moydrum_Castle "Moydrum Castle"), the site depicted on the album cover

_The Unforgettable Fire_ was released on 1 October 1984. The album took its name and much of its inspiration from a Japanese travelling exhibition of paintings and drawings at [The Peace Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Peace_Museum "The Peace Museum") in Chicago by survivors of the [atomic bombs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_bombings_of_Hiroshima_and_Nagasaki "Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki") at Hiroshima and [Nagasaki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nagasaki "Nagasaki"), Japan.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-U2byU2_151-17)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-Stokes_1996,_p._54-40) The band spent a few days driving around Ireland with photographer [Anton Corbijn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anton_Corbijn "Anton Corbijn") looking for potential locations. The castle depicted on the cover is [Moydrum Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moydrum_Castle "Moydrum Castle").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-McGee75-8) The band liked the image's ambiguity and the Irish mysticism they saw in it. The photograph, however, was a virtual copy of a picture on the cover of a 1980 book _In Ruins: The Once Great Houses of Ireland_ by [Simon Marsden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_Marsden "Simon Marsden"). It was taken from the same spot and used the same photographic techniques, but with the addition of the four band members. For this copyright infringement, the band had to pay an unknown sum to Marsden.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-mcc159-48)

"[Pride (In the Name of Love)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pride_(In_the_Name_of_Love) "Pride (In the Name of Love)")" was released as the album's lead single in September 1984, and it was at that point the band's biggest hit. It cracked the UK Top 5 and the U.S. Top 40 and would ultimately become the group's most frequently played song in concerts.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire#cite_note-49)

"[The Unforgettable Fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unforgettable_Fire_(song) "The Unforgettable Fire (song)")" was released as the second single in April 1985. The song became the band's third Top 10 hit in the UK, reaching number six on the [UK Singles Chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UK_Singles_Chart "UK Singles Chart") and number 8 on the Dutch singles chart, but did not perform as well in the U.S.
